title: Complex numbers II: exponential form, De Moivre, roots

problems.html: Write each number in exponential form r eiθr\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}reiθ with r>0r>0r>0 and −π<θ≤π-\pi<\theta\le\pi−π<θ≤π: (a) 1+i,(b) −3,(c) 2i,(d) −1−i,(e) 3−i,(f) −2+23 i.\text{(a) } 1+\mathrm{i},\quad\allowbreak \text{(b) } -3,\quad\allowbreak \text{(c) } 2\mathrm{i},\quad\allowbreak \text{(d) } -1-\mathrm{i},\quad\allowbreak \text{(e) } \sqrt3-\mathrm{i},\quad\allowbreak \text{(f) } -2+2\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i}.(a) 1+i,(b) −3,(c) 2i,(d) −1−i,(e) 3​−i,(f) −2+23​i.
hints: Exponential form needs exactly the two numbers polar form needed: the modulus rrr and an argument θ\thetaθ, since reiθ=r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=r(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)reiθ=r(cosθ+isinθ).
Sketch each point before reaching for an arctangent — it is the quadrant, not the ratio b/ab/ab/a, that decides the argument.

The window −π<θ≤π-\pi<\theta\le\pi−π<θ≤π then settles the rest: a third-quadrant point takes a negative argument, and for a point on the negative real axis, check which end of the window the inequalities actually include.
problems.format: the six arguments in order; π as pi

problems.html: Write each in Cartesian form a+iba+\mathrm{i}ba+ib: (a) 2 eiπ/3,(b) 3 eiπ,(c) 2 e−iπ/4,(d) 4 ei3π/2,(e) ei5π/6,(f) ei2π.\text{(a) } 2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/3},\quad\allowbreak \text{(b) } 3\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi},\quad\allowbreak \text{(c) } \sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi/4},\quad\allowbreak \text{(d) } 4\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}3\pi/2},\quad\allowbreak \text{(e) } \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}5\pi/6},\quad\allowbreak \text{(f) } \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi}.(a) 2eiπ/3,(b) 3eiπ,(c) 2​e−iπ/4,(d) 4ei3π/2,(e) ei5π/6,(f) ei2π. (g) Use (b) to state Euler’s identity.
hints: This is the easy direction: reiθ=rcos⁡θ+i rsin⁡θr\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=r\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\,r\sin\thetareiθ=rcosθ+irsinθ, so each part is two evaluations and a multiplication.

Several of these sit squarely on an axis, where one of the cosine and sine vanishes and there is nothing left to compute. In (d) and (f) the angle lies outside the principal window; that is harmless, since cosine and sine do not care which turn you are on.

In (c), read the cosine and sine of −π4-\tfrac{\pi}{4}−4π​ off a sketch, minding the sign of the sine, before multiplying by 2\sqrt22​; in (d) and (f), reduce the angle by a full turn first. For (g), start from your answer to (b).
problems.format: (b), (c), (d), (f) in Cartesian form

problems.html: Let z=2 eiπ/6z=2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/6}z=2eiπ/6. Write down eiπ/2z\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/2}zeiπ/2z in exponential form, and describe geometrically the effect of multiplying a complex number by (i) i\mathrm{i}i, (ii) eiπ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}eiπ, (iii) e−iπ/2\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi/2}e−iπ/2.
hints: Start from ∣eiα∣|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}|∣eiα∣: moduli multiply, so that one number decides what multiplying by eiα\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}eiα does to ∣z∣|z|∣z∣. Only the argument can move.
Multiplying by eiα\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}eiα adds α\alphaα to the argument, which is an anticlockwise turn through α\alphaα about the origin.

For the product, the argument of zzz is π6\tfrac{\pi}{6}6π​: add the turn and check that the result is still in (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π]. For (i)–(iii), write each multiplier as eiα\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}eiα and name the turn — a negative α\alphaα is a clockwise one.
problems.format: modulus and argument of the product; π as pi

problems.html: Compute, using the exponential form: (a) (1+i)4,(b) (3+i)3,(c) (1−i)6,(d) (2 eiπ/5)10.\text{(a) } (1+\mathrm{i})^{4},\quad\allowbreak \text{(b) } (\sqrt3+\mathrm{i})^{3},\quad\allowbreak \text{(c) } (1-\mathrm{i})^{6},\quad\allowbreak \text{(d) } \bigl(2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/5}\bigr)^{10}.(a) (1+i)4,(b) (3​+i)3,(c) (1−i)6,(d) (2eiπ/5)10. (e) Use De Moivre’s theorem to simplify (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)−2(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{-2}(cosθ+isinθ)−2.
hints: Convert to exponential form first. A power then costs one power of the modulus and one multiplication of the angle.

For (a), 1+i=2 eiπ/41+\mathrm{i}=\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/4}1+i=2​eiπ/4: raise the modulus to the fourth power and multiply the argument by four. In (c) the argument you land on lies outside (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π]; add a full turn before converting back.

For (e), De Moivre holds for every integer nnn, negative ones included; after applying it with n=−2n=-2n=−2, use that cosine is even and sine is odd to tidy the signs, then put θ=π4\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{4}θ=4π​ for the value that is checked.
problems.format: (a)–(d), then (e) at θ = π/4; comma-separated

problems.html: Find all the (a) square roots of i\mathrm{i}i and (b) fourth roots of 111. Plot the roots in (b) on an Argand diagram, mark the unit circle, and name the polygon they form.
hints: Write the number in exponential form, then remember that its argument is only fixed up to 2π2\pi2π — that is exactly where the extra roots come from.
For an nnnth root, take the real nnnth root of the modulus and divide θ+2πk\theta+2\pi kθ+2πk by nnn, for k=0,1,…,n−1k=0,1,\dots,n-1k=0,1,…,n−1.

In (b), write 1=ei01=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}0}1=ei0 and put n=4n=4n=4, θ=0\theta=0θ=0 into that formula for k=0,1,2,3k=0,1,2,3k=0,1,2,3; converting each root back to Cartesian form is quick on the unit circle. Plot them before naming the shape.
problems.format: (b)'s roots from 1, anticlockwise; then the polygon

problems.html: (a) State the fundamental theorem of algebra, and say what “counted with multiplicity” means. (b) How many roots in C\mathbb{C}C, counted with multiplicity, has (i) a degree-555 polynomial; (ii) z7−3=0z^{7}-3=0z7−3=0; (iii) (z−1)2(z2+1)=0(z-1)^{2}(z^{2}+1)=0(z−1)2(z2+1)=0? (c) True or false: every real cubic has at least one real root?
hints: For (a), the theorem is about how many roots a polynomial of degree nnn has in C\mathbb{C}C, and the phrase ‘with multiplicity’ is what makes the count exact: think of (z−1)2(z-1)^2(z−1)2.
So in (b) the only work is finding the degree. In (iii) do not solve anything — just add up the degrees of the factors, remembering that (z−1)2(z-1)^2(z−1)2 contributes two.
For (c): a real cubic has three roots counted with multiplicity, and the conjugate-pair property says how its non-real roots must occur. Ask whether all three roots can be accounted for that way.
problems.format: (b)(i), (ii), (iii), then (c): true or false

problems.html: Using cos⁡θ=12(eiθ+e−iθ)\cos\theta=\tfrac12(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}+\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta})cosθ=21​(eiθ+e−iθ), evaluate cos⁡(i)\cos(\mathrm{i})cos(i) in terms of e\mathrm{e}e. (The general identity cos⁡(ix)=cosh⁡x\cos(\mathrm{i}x)=\cosh xcos(ix)=coshx is built up in Exercise 2.9.)
hints: Do not try to picture this one; simply substitute θ=i\theta=\mathrm{i}θ=i into the formula you are given.
The exponents become i⋅i=−1\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}=-1i⋅i=−1 and −i⋅i=1-\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}=1−i⋅i=1, so both exponentials turn into ordinary real numbers.

Put those two real exponentials back into the formula and recognise the result as a hyperbolic function of a real number, then evaluate it to four decimal places. A cosine of a real angle never exceeds 111; this one does.
problems.format: the value of cos(i), to 4 d.p.

problems.html: (a) Write 5cos⁡(ωt+π3)5\cos(\omega t+\tfrac{\pi}{3})5cos(ωt+3π​) and 2sin⁡ωt2\sin\omega t2sinωt as phasors P=A eiφP=A\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}P=Aeiφ. (b) The phasor 3 e−iπ/23\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi/2}3e−iπ/2 represents which real signal Acos⁡(ωt+φ)A\cos(\omega t+\varphi)Acos(ωt+φ)?
hints: A phasor records only the amplitude and the phase of a cosine, discarding the eiωt\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}eiωt that every term in the problem shares.

Everything must be written as a cosine first. A sine is a cosine shifted by a quarter period, but which way? Find the φ\varphiφ with sin⁡ωt=cos⁡(ωt+φ)\sin\omega t=\cos(\omega t+\varphi)sinωt=cos(ωt+φ) by checking ωt=π2\omega t=\tfrac{\pi}{2}ωt=2π​, where the sine peaks.

Only (a) is checked: each phasor A eiφA\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}Aeiφ contributes its amplitude AAA and its phase φ\varphiφ, read off the cosine form. For (b), run the same reading backwards, then ask whether the cosine you get has a simpler name.
problems.format: amplitude and phase of each in (a); π as pi

problems.html: Let z=3+iz=\sqrt3+\mathrm{i}z=3​+i and w=1+iw=1+\mathrm{i}w=1+i. Write zzz and www in exponential form, then find zwzwzw and z/wz/wz/w in both exponential and Cartesian form.
hints: Convert both numbers to exponential form first; the index laws then do all of the work.

Both numbers lie in the first quadrant, so each argument is an arctangent of a ratio you should recognise: 13\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}3​1​ for zzz and 111 for www. Then multiply moduli and add arguments, or divide and subtract.

Only the arguments are checked: put π6\tfrac{\pi}{6}6π​ and π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}4π​ over a common denominator before adding or subtracting, and mind which comes first in the quotient. For the Cartesian forms, expanding (3+i)(1+i)(\sqrt3+\mathrm{i})(1+\mathrm{i})(3​+i)(1+i) and using the conjugate on the quotient gives a check — the two routes must agree.
problems.format: the arguments of zw and z/w; π as pi

problems.html: (a) Rotate z=3+4iz=3+4\mathrm{i}z=3+4i anticlockwise by π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​ about the origin, and then (separately) clockwise by π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​. (b) Rotate 2+2i2+2\mathrm{i}2+2i anticlockwise by π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}4π​. Give exact Cartesian answers.
hints: Anticlockwise by π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​ is multiplication by eiπ/2=i\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/2}=\mathrm{i}eiπ/2=i; clockwise by the same angle is multiplication by −i-\mathrm{i}−i.

So (a) is two one-line multiplications: expand i(3+4i)\mathrm{i}(3+4\mathrm{i})i(3+4i) and −i(3+4i)-\mathrm{i}(3+4\mathrm{i})−i(3+4i), using i2=−1\mathrm{i}^{2}=-1i2=−1, with no trigonometry involved at all.

Check (a) geometrically: both images should still have modulus 555 and sit a quarter turn either side of 3+4i3+4\mathrm{i}3+4i. For (b), write 2+2i2+2\mathrm{i}2+2i in exponential form, add π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}4π​ to its argument, and convert back.
problems.format: the two rotations of z in (a)

problems.html: Prove by induction that (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)n=cos⁡nθ+isin⁡nθ(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{n}=\cos n\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin n\theta(cosθ+isinθ)n=cosnθ+isinnθ for all integers n≥1n\ge1n≥1. (Pure-maths.)
hints: Induction on nnn: verify the case n=1n=1n=1, then assume the statement at n=kn=kn=k and derive it at n=k+1n=k+1n=k+1.

The inductive step starts (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)k+1=(cos⁡kθ+isin⁡kθ)(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{k+1}=(\cos k\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin k\theta)(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)(cosθ+isinθ)k+1=(coskθ+isinkθ)(cosθ+isinθ), using the hypothesis on the first factor.

Both factors have modulus 111, so the polar product rule — multiply moduli, add arguments — finishes the inductive step without a single trigonometric expansion. For the checked value, apply the result with n=6n=6n=6 and θ=π6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}θ=6π​.
problems.format: the value of (cos θ + i sin θ)⁶ at θ = π/6

problems.html: Compute (a) (1+i)8(1+\mathrm{i})^{8}(1+i)8 and (b) (3+i)6(\sqrt3+\mathrm{i})^{6}(3​+i)6 using De Moivre’s theorem.
hints: Convert, raise, convert back. The binomial theorem would need nine terms for the first of these; De Moivre needs one line.

For (a), 1+i=2 eiπ/41+\mathrm{i}=\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/4}1+i=2​eiπ/4; for (b), find the modulus and argument of 3+i\sqrt3+\mathrm{i}3​+i the same way, from a sketch. Then raise each modulus to the power and multiply each argument by it.

Reduce each final argument to the window (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π] before converting back. Both come out as whole multiples of π\piπ, so both answers are real; whether the multiple is even or odd decides the sign.
problems.format: (1+i)⁸ and (√3+i)⁶, comma-separated

problems.html: Find (a) the cube roots of 888 and (b) the fourth roots of −16-16−16. In each case give exact Cartesian values and describe the polygon they form on the Argand diagram.
hints: Write the right-hand side in exponential form, then apply the root formula: the real nnnth root of the modulus, and arguments (θ+2πk)/n(\theta+2\pi k)/n(θ+2πk)/n.
In (a), 8=8 ei08=8\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}0}8=8ei0, so θ=0\theta=0θ=0 and the arguments are 0,2π3,4π30,\tfrac{2\pi}{3},\tfrac{4\pi}{3}0,32π​,34π​; the modulus is whatever the formula makes of 888.

In (b) start from −16=16 eiπ-16=16\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}−16=16eiπ — that non-zero starting angle is what turns the picture away from the axes. All nnn roots share a single modulus, the real nnnth root of the right-hand side's modulus, which is why they always sit on one circle.
problems.format: the modulus of the roots in (a), then in (b)

problems.html: Find all sixth roots of unity in Cartesian form, and verify that they sum to zero. Why does this generalise to all n≥2n\ge2n≥2?
hints: The nnnth roots of unity are ei2πk/n\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi k/n}ei2πk/n for k=0,…,n−1k=0,\dots,n-1k=0,…,n−1; here that means six points a sixth of a turn apart.

With wk=ei2πk/6w_k=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi k/6}wk​=ei2πk/6, the real part of each root is cos⁡2πk6\cos\tfrac{2\pi k}{6}cos62πk​: read the six values off the unit circle, a sixth of a turn at a time, and keep them in order of kkk.

The roots come in conjugate pairs, so the imaginary parts cancel in the sum, and your six real parts should add to 000, as the statement says. For general nnn, sum the geometric series with ratio ω=ei2π/n\omega=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi/n}ω=ei2π/n, then ask what ωn\omega^{n}ωn is and why the formula is allowed at all.
problems.format: Re of the roots, k=0,…,5; fractions, commas

problems.html: The fast Fourier transform is built from the “twiddle factors” WNk=e−i2πk/NW_{N}^{k}=\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}2\pi k/N}WNk​=e−i2πk/N. Take N=8N=8N=8. (a) Write W81W_{8}^{1}W81​ in Cartesian form. (b) Show that W8k+4=− W8kW_{8}^{k+4}=-\,W_{8}^{k}W8k+4​=−W8k​ for every integer kkk (the symmetry that halves the FFT’s work). (c) Give the modulus and argument of W83W_{8}^{3}W83​.
hints: Every twiddle factor is e\mathrm{e}e raised to a purely imaginary power. What is ∣eiϕ∣|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\phi}|∣eiϕ∣ for real ϕ\phiϕ, and so where in the plane do all of them lie?

For (b), split the exponent: e−i2π(k+4)/8=e−i2πk/8⋅e−iπ\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}2\pi(k+4)/8}=\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}2\pi k/8}\cdot\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi}e−i2π(k+4)/8=e−i2πk/8⋅e−iπ, then evaluate the second factor.

For (c), W83W_{8}^{3}W83​ is already in the form r eiθr\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}reiθ: substitute k=3k=3k=3 and N=8N=8N=8, read off rrr and θ\thetaθ, and check that θ\thetaθ lies in (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π].
problems.format: modulus and argument of W₈³; π as pi

problems.html: Using De Moivre and the binomial theorem, show that cos⁡3θ=4cos⁡3θ−3cos⁡θ\cos 3\theta=4\cos^{3}\theta-3\cos\thetacos3θ=4cos3θ−3cosθ and sin⁡3θ=3sin⁡θ−4sin⁡3θ\sin 3\theta=3\sin\theta-4\sin^{3}\thetasin3θ=3sinθ−4sin3θ.
hints: Expand (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)3(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{3}(cosθ+isinθ)3 with the binomial theorem, tracking the powers of i\mathrm{i}i carefully.
By De Moivre that expansion also equals cos⁡3θ+isin⁡3θ\cos3\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin3\thetacos3θ+isin3θ, so match real parts against real and imaginary against imaginary.

Collect the real terms and the imaginary terms before substituting anything: those four coefficients are what is checked, and each power i2\mathrm{i}^{2}i2 or i3\mathrm{i}^{3}i3 is where a sign enters. Replacing sin⁡2θ\sin^{2}\thetasin2θ by 1−cos⁡2θ1-\cos^{2}\theta1−cos2θ (and cos⁡2θ\cos^{2}\thetacos2θ by 1−sin⁡2θ1-\sin^{2}\theta1−sin2θ) then reaches the stated forms, a check on those signs.
problems.format: a,b,c,d: Re=aC³+bCS², Im=cC²S+dS³; C=cosθ, S=sinθ

problems.html: (a) Show cos⁡(ix)=cosh⁡x\cos(\mathrm{i}x)=\cosh xcos(ix)=coshx and sin⁡(ix)=isinh⁡x\sin(\mathrm{i}x)=\mathrm{i}\sinh xsin(ix)=isinhx. (b) Hence evaluate cos⁡(iln⁡2)\cos(\mathrm{i}\ln 2)cos(iln2) exactly.
hints: Use the inverse Euler formulas and substitute θ=ix\theta=\mathrm{i}xθ=ix; the imaginary unit in the exponent then cancels against the one in the argument.
For the sine you will need 1i=−i\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{i}}=-\mathrm{i}i1​=−i to tidy up the factor in front.

For (b), part (a) turns cos⁡(iln⁡2)\cos(\mathrm{i}\ln 2)cos(iln2) into a hyperbolic function of ln⁡2\ln 2ln2. Write that out in exponentials; the log laws then turn eln⁡2\mathrm{e}^{\ln 2}eln2 and e−ln⁡2\mathrm{e}^{-\ln 2}e−ln2 into ordinary numbers.
problems.format: the value of cos(i·ln2), as a fraction

problems.html: (a) Combine 3cos⁡ωt+4sin⁡ωt3\cos\omega t+4\sin\omega t3cosωt+4sinωt into a single sinusoid Rcos⁡(ωt−α)R\cos(\omega t-\alpha)Rcos(ωt−α). (b) Combine 2cos⁡ωt+2cos⁡(ωt+π2)2\cos\omega t+2\cos(\omega t+\tfrac{\pi}{2})2cosωt+2cos(ωt+2π​) likewise.
hints: Turn every term into a cosine, take its phasor, add the phasors as complex numbers, and read the answer off the sum.

sin⁡ωt=cos⁡(ωt−π2)\sin\omega t=\cos(\omega t-\tfrac{\pi}{2})sinωt=cos(ωt−2π​), so a sine term contributes a phasor with argument −π2-\tfrac{\pi}{2}−2π​ — that is, a negative multiple of i\mathrm{i}i. In (b) no conversion is needed: both terms are cosines already.

The modulus of the phasor sum is the amplitude RRR; its argument is −α-\alpha−α, since the target is written Rcos⁡(ωt−α)R\cos(\omega t-\alpha)Rcos(ωt−α). Check the quadrant before using an arctangent, and notice that RRR is not the sum of the two original amplitudes.
problems.format: R and α in (a); α to 3 d.p.

problems.html: (a) Solve w3=−27iw^{3}=-27\mathrm{i}w3=−27i, giving the three roots in exponential and Cartesian form. (b) Solve w3=1+iw^{3}=1+\mathrm{i}w3=1+i, leaving the roots in exponential form, and check that each root is the previous one rotated through 2π3\tfrac{2\pi}{3}32π​ about the origin.
hints: Put each right-hand side into exponential form first: −27i-27\mathrm{i}−27i sits on the negative imaginary axis, and 1+i1+\mathrm{i}1+i in the first quadrant.

Then the root formula: the modulus of each root is the real cube root of the modulus, and the arguments are (θ+2πk)/3(\theta+2\pi k)/3(θ+2πk)/3 for k=0,1,2k=0,1,2k=0,1,2. In (a) one root comes out purely imaginary — a useful check on the arithmetic.

Enter the arguments exactly as (θ+2πk)/3(\theta+2\pi k)/3(θ+2πk)/3 gives them for k=0,1,2k=0,1,2k=0,1,2, with θ\thetaθ the principal argument of the right-hand side: simplified, but not shifted back into (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π]. For the rotation check in (b), compare consecutive arguments: all three roots share one modulus, so a fixed difference is a rotation about the origin.
problems.format: (a); (b): args k=0,1,2 in pi, unreduced, not (−π,π]

problems.html: The argument of 5−12i5-12\mathrm{i}5−12i is not a standard angle, so the exponential method is awkward. Instead find both square roots of 5−12i5-12\mathrm{i}5−12i in Cartesian form by equating real and imaginary parts of (a+ib)2(a+\mathrm{i}b)^{2}(a+ib)2, and verify by squaring.
hints: Set (a+ib)2=5−12i(a+\mathrm{i}b)^{2}=5-12\mathrm{i}(a+ib)2=5−12i, expand the left side, and match real and imaginary parts.
That gives a2−b2=5a^{2}-b^{2}=5a2−b2=5 and 2ab=−122ab=-122ab=−12. A third equation comes free from the moduli: a2+b2=∣5−12i∣a^{2}+b^{2}=|5-12\mathrm{i}|a2+b2=∣5−12i∣.
Adding and subtracting the two equations in a2a^{2}a2 and b2b^{2}b2 isolates each. Then let the sign of 2ab2ab2ab decide whether aaa and bbb share a sign or not.
problems.format: both square roots; positive real part first

problems.html: (a) Verify that z=2iz=2\mathrm{i}z=2i is a root of z2+4z^{2}+4z2+4, and write down the other. (b) Factor z4+4z^{4}+4z4+4 into two real quadratics. [Hint: find the four roots first.]
hints: For (a), substitute z=2iz=2\mathrm{i}z=2i and check that you get 000. Then look at the coefficients of z2+4z^{2}+4z2+4: what does their being real guarantee about the roots?
For (b) solve z4=−4z^{4}=-4z4=−4 with the root formula — the four roots come out as ±1±i\pm1\pm\mathrm{i}±1±i.

Check (a) the way (b) is built: if www is your other root, (z−2i)(z−w)(z-2\mathrm{i})(z-w)(z−2i)(z−w) must multiply out to z2+4z^{2}+4z2+4. In (b), pair each root with its conjugate — (z−(1+i))(z−(1−i))\bigl(z-(1+\mathrm{i})\bigr)\bigl(z-(1-\mathrm{i})\bigr)(z−(1+i))(z−(1−i)) multiplies out with no i\mathrm{i}i surviving.
problems.format: the other root of z²+4

problems.html: Find all z∈Cz\in\mathbb{C}z∈C with z2=z‾z^{2}=\overline{z}z2=z.
hints: Polar form is far easier here than Cartesian: write z=r eiθz=r\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}z=reiθ and note that zˉ=r e−iθ\bar z=r\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}zˉ=re−iθ.
Matching moduli gives r2=rr^{2}=rr2=r. Deal with the case r=0r=0r=0 separately, before you divide by rrr.

Matching arguments gives 2θ≡−θ2\theta\equiv-\theta2θ≡−θ modulo 2π2\pi2π, so 3θ3\theta3θ is a whole number of turns. Count the distinct θ\thetaθ that allows, and do not lose the solution you set aside.

problems.html: Use the inverse Euler formula to write sin⁡4θ\sin^{4}\thetasin4θ as a sum of cosines of multiples of θ\thetaθ.

cosh⁡(ix)=12(eix+e−ix)\cosh(\mathrm{i}x)=\tfrac12\left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}x}+\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}x}\right)cosh(ix)=21​(eix+e−ix) is literally the formula for cos⁡x\cos xcosx; the sine case picks up a factor of i\mathrm{i}i along the way.

For the evaluations, the pair you have just proved runs the wrong way: sin⁡(2i)\sin(2\mathrm{i})sin(2i) and cos⁡(πi)\cos(\pi\mathrm{i})cos(πi) are trigonometric functions of imaginary arguments, which is what Exercise 2.9 handled. questions.stem: A student writes: 'by De Moivre with n=12n=\tfrac12n=21​, the square root of eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ is eiθ/2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta/2}eiθ/2.' What is wrong?
options: Nothing — De Moivre holds for every real nnn.
De Moivre is proved for integer nnn, and in any case a non-zero number has two square roots, not one.
The formula is wrong; the square root is 12eiθ\tfrac12\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}21​eiθ.
eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ has a square root only when θ\thetaθ is a multiple of 2π2\pi2π.
questions.hint: Two things are worth checking: the values of nnn the theorem was actually proved for, and how many square roots a non-zero complex number has.
questions.why: Two separate faults. The theorem as proved covers n∈Zn\in\mathbb{Z}n∈Z, so n=12n=\tfrac12n=21​ is outside its range — the step is unjustified even where the value happens to be right. More seriously it loses a root: the argument of eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ is fixed only up to 2π2\pi2π, so the square roots are ei(θ+2πk)/2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\theta+2\pi k)/2}ei(θ+2πk)/2 for k=0,1k=0,1k=0,1, namely eiθ/2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta/2}eiθ/2 and −eiθ/2-\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta/2}−eiθ/2. The student's value is one of the two.

questions.stem: Does eiθ=eiφ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}eiθ=eiφ force θ=φ\theta=\varphiθ=φ, for real θ\thetaθ and φ\varphiφ?
options: Yes, provided both angles are real.
No: an argument is fixed only up to a whole turn, so θ\thetaθ and φ\varphiφ may differ by a multiple of 2π2\pi2π.
No, because eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ is not one-to-one on any interval at all.
Yes — the exponential function is one-to-one.
questions.hint: Try θ=0\theta=0θ=0 and φ=2π\varphi=2\piφ=2π.
questions.why: The simplest counterexample is ei0=ei2π=1\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}0}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi}=1ei0=ei2π=1. The real exponential really is one-to-one, which is why the failure catches people out; but θ↦eiθ\theta\mapsto\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}θ↦eiθ wraps the real line repeatedly around the unit circle. It is one-to-one on any half-open interval of length 2π2\pi2π — which is precisely why the principal argument is defined on (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π] — so the last option overstates the failure. This ambiguity is not a defect: it is the source of every extra nnnth root.

questions.stem: Where in the Argand plane do the five fifth roots of a non-zero complex number zzz lie?
options: At five different distances from the origin, one for each root.
At the vertices of a regular pentagon, but only when zzz is real and positive.
Spread along a straight line through the origin.
At the vertices of a regular pentagon on the circle of radius ∣z∣1/5|z|^{1/5}∣z∣1/5.
questions.hint: All nnn roots share one modulus, so they share one circle. What is left to tell them apart, and by how much do consecutive ones differ?
questions.why: Every root has the same modulus, the real fifth root of ∣z∣|z|∣z∣, so all five sit on one circle. Consecutive arguments differ by 2π5\tfrac{2\pi}{5}52π​, because each root is the previous one multiplied by ei2π/5\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi/5}ei2π/5 — a rotation. Equal spacing on a circle is exactly a regular polygon. A non-zero argument for zzz turns the whole pentagon to match, but cannot change its shape, so the restriction in the last option is unnecessary.

questions.stem: Combining 3cos⁡ωt+4sin⁡ωt3\cos\omega t+4\sin\omega t3cosωt+4sinωt into a single sinusoid Rcos⁡(ωt−α)R\cos(\omega t-\alpha)Rcos(ωt−α), what is the amplitude RRR?
options: 333, since the cosine term is the one in phase.
7\sqrt77​.
555, the modulus of the phasor sum 3−4i3-4\mathrm{i}3−4i.
777, the sum of the two amplitudes.
questions.hint: Write 4sin⁡ωt4\sin\omega t4sinωt as a cosine with a phase shift, then add the two *phasors* as complex numbers rather than adding the amplitudes.
questions.why: Amplitudes add only when the two terms are in phase, and these are a quarter-turn apart. Writing 4sin⁡ωt=4cos⁡ ⁣(ωt−π2)4\sin\omega t=4\cos\!\left(\omega t-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)4sinωt=4cos(ωt−2π​) gives phasors 333 and −4i-4\mathrm{i}−4i, whose sum is 3−4i3-4\mathrm{i}3−4i — the 333–444–555 triangle again, so R=5R=5R=5. The phase follows from the argument: α=arctan⁡43≈0.927\alpha=\arctan\tfrac43\approx0.927α=arctan34​≈0.927. Adding to 777 would be right only if the phase difference were zero, and 7\sqrt77​ corresponds to no step in the calculation at all.

questions.stem: How many cube roots does the number 000 have?
options: One, namely 000 itself.
Three, like every other complex number.
Infinitely many.
None.
questions.hint: Put r=0r=0r=0 into ρ=r1/n\rho=r^{1/n}ρ=r1/n, then count how many *distinct* numbers the root formula can produce.
questions.why: The root formula wk=ρ ei(θ+2πk)/nw_k=\rho\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\theta+2\pi k)/n}wk​=ρei(θ+2πk)/n needs a modulus ρ=r1/n\rho=r^{1/n}ρ=r1/n. When r=0r=0r=0 that is 000 for every kkk, so all three candidates collapse onto the same number and the distinct arguments become meaningless. Zero is the single exception to 'every complex number has exactly nnn nnnth roots', and it is what makes the corresponding true/false item on the exercise sheet false. The fundamental theorem is untouched: z3=0z^3=0z3=0 still has three roots counted with multiplicity, all of them 000.

questions.stem: Substituting θ=ix\theta=\mathrm{i}xθ=ix turns trigonometric identities into hyperbolic ones. What single fact explains why the two families differ by signs?
options: It is a coincidence with no underlying reason.
sin⁡(ix)=isinh⁡x\sin(\mathrm{i}x)=\mathrm{i}\sinh xsin(ix)=isinhx, so squaring a sine introduces a factor of −1-1−1.
The hyperbolic functions are not periodic.
Hyperbolic functions are defined on a hyperbola rather than a circle.
questions.hint: Substitute θ=ix\theta=\mathrm{i}xθ=ix into cos⁡\coscos and into sin⁡\sinsin separately, and see which of the two picks up a stray factor.
questions.why: Cosines transfer unchanged, since cos⁡(ix)=cosh⁡x\cos(\mathrm{i}x)=\cosh xcos(ix)=coshx with no stray factor. Sines do not: sin⁡(ix)=isinh⁡x\sin(\mathrm{i}x)=\mathrm{i}\sinh xsin(ix)=isinhx, so sin⁡2(ix)=(isinh⁡x)2=−sinh⁡2x\sin^{2}(\mathrm{i}x)=(\mathrm{i}\sinh x)^{2}=-\sinh^{2}xsin2(ix)=(isinhx)2=−sinh2x. Every sign difference between the two families traces back to that one squared i\mathrm{i}i — the pattern usually quoted as Osborn's rule. The first and third options are perfectly true statements about hyperbolic functions, but neither of them predicts which signs flip.

questions.stem: To find (1+i)8(1+\mathrm{i})^{8}(1+i)8 a student writes (1+i)8=cos⁡8θ+isin⁡8θ(1+\mathrm{i})^{8}=\cos 8\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin 8\theta(1+i)8=cos8θ+isin8θ with θ=π4\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{4}θ=4π​, citing De Moivre. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: 1+i1+\mathrm{i}1+i has argument π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}4π​, so this is correct.

The modulus was dropped. Since 1+i=2(cos⁡π4+isin⁡π4)1+\mathrm{i}=\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{4}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)1+i=2​(cos4π​+isin4π​), the answer carries a factor (2)8=16\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^{8}=16(2​)8=16.
The argument must first be reduced to the principal range, which changes the value.
De Moivre's theorem holds only for n≤3n\le 3n≤3.
questions.hint: Put 1+i1+\mathrm{i}1+i into full polar form before raising it to a power. Is its modulus 111?
questions.why: De Moivre's theorem is a statement about cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\thetacosθ+isinθ, a number of modulus 111. Here the modulus is ∣1+i∣=2\left|1+\mathrm{i}\right|=\sqrt{2}∣1+i∣=2​, and it does not come along for free: the full polar form is 2(cos⁡π4+isin⁡π4)\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{4}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)2​(cos4π​+isin4π​), so the eighth power is (2)8(cos⁡2π+isin⁡2π)=16\left(\sqrt2\right)^{8}\left(\cos 2\pi+\mathrm{i}\sin 2\pi\right)=16(2​)8(cos2π+isin2π)=16. A direct check agrees: (1+i)2=2i(1+\mathrm{i})^{2}=2\mathrm{i}(1+i)2=2i, so (1+i)8=(2i)4=16(1+\mathrm{i})^{8}=(2\mathrm{i})^{4}=16(1+i)8=(2i)4=16. The theorem holds for every integer nnn, and reducing an argument to the principal range changes how a number is written, never what it is.

questions.stem: Expanding (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)3\left(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta\right)^{3}(cosθ+isinθ)3 by the binomial theorem and comparing real parts with cos⁡3θ\cos 3\thetacos3θ gives which identity?
options: cos⁡3θ=cos⁡3θ−3cos⁡θsin⁡2θ\cos 3\theta=\cos^{3}\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^{2}\thetacos3θ=cos3θ−3cosθsin2θ
cos⁡3θ=3cos⁡θsin⁡2θ−cos⁡3θ\cos 3\theta=3\cos\theta\sin^{2}\theta-\cos^{3}\thetacos3θ=3cosθsin2θ−cos3θ
cos⁡3θ=3cos⁡3θ−cos⁡θ\cos 3\theta=3\cos^{3}\theta-\cos\thetacos3θ=3cos3θ−cosθ
cos⁡3θ=cos⁡3θ+3cos⁡θsin⁡2θ\cos 3\theta=\cos^{3}\theta+3\cos\theta\sin^{2}\thetacos3θ=cos3θ+3cosθsin2θ
questions.hint: Expand the bracket, keeping track of i2=−1\mathrm{i}^{2}=-1i2=−1 and i3=−i\mathrm{i}^{3}=-\mathrm{i}i3=−i, then keep only the terms with no i\mathrm{i}i left in them.
questions.why: Writing c=cos⁡θc=\cos\thetac=cosθ and s=sin⁡θs=\sin\thetas=sinθ, the expansion is c3+3ic2s−3cs2−is3c^{3}+3\mathrm{i}c^{2}s-3cs^{2}-\mathrm{i}s^{3}c3+3ic2s−3cs2−is3, since i2=−1\mathrm{i}^{2}=-1i2=−1 and i3=−i\mathrm{i}^{3}=-\mathrm{i}i3=−i. De Moivre says this equals cos⁡3θ+isin⁡3θ\cos3\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin3\thetacos3θ+isin3θ, so matching real parts gives cos⁡3θ=c3−3cs2\cos3\theta=c^{3}-3cs^{2}cos3θ=c3−3cs2 — and matching imaginary parts gives sin⁡3θ=3c2s−s3\sin3\theta=3c^{2}s-s^{3}sin3θ=3c2s−s3 free of charge. The minus sign is the whole point: it comes from i2\mathrm{i}^{2}i2, and dropping it is the usual slip. Substituting s2=1−c2s^{2}=1-c^{2}s2=1−c2 turns the answer into the familiar cos⁡3θ=4cos⁡3θ−3cos⁡θ\cos3\theta=4\cos^{3}\theta-3\cos\thetacos3θ=4cos3θ−3cosθ.

questions.stem: How many roots has (x−1)2(x+3)=0(x-1)^{2}(x+3)=0(x−1)2(x+3)=0 in C\mathbb{C}C?
options: Three, counted with multiplicity: 111 twice and −3-3−3 once.
One, since only x=1x=1x=1 makes a repeated factor vanish.
Three, and all three are distinct, since the degree is 333.
Two, namely 111 and −3-3−3.
questions.hint: Read off the degree, then ask how many times each factor asks its root to vanish. The fundamental theorem counts in a particular way — which?
questions.why: The fundamental theorem of algebra says a degree-nnn polynomial has exactly nnn roots in C\mathbb{C}C counted with multiplicity, and this one has degree 333. The distinct roots number only two, 111 and −3-3−3; the count reaches three because the factor (x−1)2(x-1)^{2}(x−1)2 asks x=1x=1x=1 to be a root twice. So "two" and "three" are both right answers to different questions, and the theorem is about the second. Distinctness is not promised — x2−2x+1=(x−1)2x^{2}-2x+1=(x-1)^{2}x2−2x+1=(x−1)2 has its two roots at the same place — and x=−3x=-3x=−3 is a root just as much as x=1x=1x=1 is.
